name: Kernow Rating — What This Rating Means Phrasebank

descriptions: Learning the serve, the score and the court. The rating is a starting picture rather than a measure of standard.
Everything is new at this stage. The rating records where you are starting from, and nothing more.
The basics are still being learned — where to stand, when to serve, how the scoring works. That is exactly as it should be.
This is a first snapshot. It marks the beginning of the picture rather than judging the standard.
At this stage the game is mostly about getting the ball in play and learning the rules that go with it.
The rating is a baseline to measure from. Nobody's first assessment says much about how far they will go.
Early days. The serve, the score and the shape of the court are the things being learned right now.
Rallies are short and the rules are still settling. That is normal, and it changes quickly.
This is the starting point of your record, not a verdict on your game.
The court, the score and the serve are the priorities. Everything else follows from those.
summary: Every player on the court started exactly here, including the ones who now look effortless.
The fastest gains in pickleball come at this stage, so expect this picture to move quickly.
Getting the ball in play consistently is the whole job for now, and it is worth more than any clever shot.
Nothing here needs fixing yet. It needs repeating until it feels normal.
Court time matters more than technique at this point. Play as often as you can.
The scoring is the hardest part for most people at this stage, and it does become automatic.
Focus on one thing per session rather than everything at once.
Your rating will move faster now than at any later point in your playing life.
Confidence tends to arrive before consistency. Both are coming.
This is the stage where playing is the practice. Games will teach you more than drills for a while.
closing: This rating reflects where your game is today, not where it can go. Bring it back in a few months and expect the picture to have moved.
One focus area at a time is plenty. Come back for a reassessment once it starts to feel automatic.
Keep playing to your strengths while you work on the focus area — the fastest progress usually comes from doing both at once.
Play as much as you can between now and your next assessment. At this stage, court time does most of the work.
Do not worry about the number. Worry about whether the game is getting more enjoyable.
Come back in a couple of months. Early ratings move faster than later ones.
Ask someone more experienced to hit with you occasionally. It is the quickest way to learn what good feels like.
Nothing in this report is a criticism. It is a starting line.
Keep it simple: serve, return, get the ball back. The rest can wait.
The players who improve fastest are the ones who keep turning up. That is the whole secret at this stage.

descriptions: Rallies are beginning to hold together and the basic shot shapes are in place. Points are still decided mostly by unforced errors rather than by tactics.
The shots are recognisable and rallies last longer, but most points still end with a mistake rather than a decision.
You can keep a rally going now. Errors, rather than tactics, still decide who wins the point.
Basic technique is settling. The next step is cutting out the free points you give away.
Rallies hold together for a few shots at a time. Consistency is the thing standing between you and the next band.
The shot shapes are there on both wings. Repeating them under pressure is what comes next.
Points tend to be lost rather than won at this stage, which is normal and very fixable.
You have the shots to play a rally out. Playing several in a row is the current limit.
The game is starting to look like pickleball rather than a series of separate shots.
Technique is no longer the main problem. Reliability is.
summary: There is a solid foundation here, and it is the platform everything else builds on.
The shots you have are enough to compete at this level once they repeat more often.
Cutting errors will move your rating faster than adding anything new.
Rallies are lasting longer, which is the clearest sign of progress at this stage.
You have more of the game than your results probably suggest.
The gap between your best shot and your average one is where the improvement is.
Nothing here needs rebuilding. It needs repeating.
Consistency is the only real barrier between you and the next band.
You can already play the shots; the next step is choosing when to play them.
This is the stage where patience starts to beat power, and that shift is worth a lot of points.
closing: This rating reflects where your game is today, not where it can go. Bring it back in a few months and expect the picture to have moved.
One focus area at a time is plenty. Come back for a reassessment once it starts to feel automatic.
Keep playing to your strengths while you work on the focus area — the fastest progress usually comes from doing both at once.
Count your unforced errors across a game or two. It is the quickest way to see where the points are going.
Pick one shot to make boring and reliable before your next assessment.
Play some games where your only aim is to keep the ball in. The score usually takes care of itself.
Come back for a reassessment once rallies routinely last six or seven shots.
Consistency is unglamorous, and it moves ratings faster than anything else.
Drill a little, play a lot. At this stage both still count.
If one number in this report annoys you, that is usually the right one to work on.

descriptions: Serves, returns and baseline rallies are reliable enough to sustain a point. The soft game and the move forward to the kitchen are the main limits.
The back-court game holds up. Getting forward and playing softly at the line is where the ceiling currently sits.
You can sustain a rally comfortably from the baseline. The kitchen is the part of the court still to be won.
Serve, return and groundstrokes are dependable. The third shot and the soft game are the next frontier.
Points last as long as they need to at the back. The limit is what happens when they move forward.
The hard game is in place; the soft game is the missing half.
Rallies are reliable rather than fragile now. Transition to the line is the remaining gap.
You have the shots to hold a point together. Where you play them from is the current limit.
Baseline play is solid. Most of your lost points now happen on the way in, or at the line.
The foundations are done. The soft game is what separates this band from the next.
summary: Several parts of your profile already create problems for opponents at your level.
The hard part is behind you. What remains is a different kind of skill rather than a harder version of the same one.
Time spent at the kitchen line will pay back faster than anything else you could practise.
You have enough game to beat players above you on a good night.
The soft game is the single biggest lever available to you at this stage.
Most of your rating is now decided by what happens after the third shot, not before it.
Your baseline game is doing its job. The next points come from further forward.
Patience, rather than technique, is what is being tested at this level.
You can build points now. The next step is finishing them.
This is the band where players either learn the soft game or stall, and the choice is usually deliberate.
closing: This rating reflects where your game is today, not where it can go. Bring it back in a few months and expect the picture to have moved.
One focus area at a time is plenty. Come back for a reassessment once it starts to feel automatic.
Keep playing to your strengths while you work on the focus area — the fastest progress usually comes from doing both at once.
Spend a session at the kitchen line and nowhere else. It is the fastest way through this band.
Come back for a reassessment once the third shot feels like a choice rather than a gamble.
If you only change one thing, make it the amount of time you spend playing soft.
The players who move past this band are the ones who got comfortable slowing the game down.
Ask a stronger pair to dink with you for ten minutes. It is worth an hour of drills.
Keep the baseline game as it is. It is not what is holding you back.
One focus area, six weeks, then reassess. That is usually enough to see the shift.

descriptions: Points can be built deliberately — third shots, dinks and resets work more often than not. Quality drops away when the pace lifts or the rally runs long.
You construct points rather than react to them. Holding that construction under pressure is the current limit.
The soft game and the transition both work. They stop working when the rally speeds up or drags on.
Third shots, dinks and resets are all available. Repeating them when it matters is the remaining gap.
You can play the right shot most of the time. Doing it on the twelfth ball is what comes next.
The tools are all there. Durability under pressure is what is missing.
Deliberate point construction is in place, and it holds until the intensity rises.
You have a complete club game on a good day. The gap is between your good days and your average ones.
Points are built rather than stumbled into. Pace and length are what break them up.
Everything works in a settled rally. The next band is about keeping it working in an unsettled one.
summary: Your strongest skills already let you influence rallies rather than just react to them.
You have the shots for the next band. Holding them under pressure is what is being asked now.
The difference between you and the band above is durability, not repertoire.
Most of what you need is already in your game. It needs to survive contact with a fast rally.
Your ceiling is clearly higher than your average, which is a good problem to have.
Opponents have to work for their points against you on a good day.
What you can do is no longer the question. What you can repeat is.
This is the band where fitness and composure start to matter as much as technique.
You can already beat players rated above you. Doing it twice in a row is the next step.
The gap to the next band is measured in consistency, not in new skills.
closing: This rating reflects where your game is today, not where it can go. Bring it back in a few months and expect the picture to have moved.
One focus area at a time is plenty. Come back for a reassessment once it starts to feel automatic.
Keep playing to your strengths while you work on the focus area — the fastest progress usually comes from doing both at once.
Practise at the end of a session rather than the start. That is where your gap actually lives.
Play the tight scores deliberately. Games from 8–8 are worth more to you than games from 0–0.
Come back for a reassessment once your third game feels like your first.
You do not need new shots. You need the ones you have to survive a long rally.
Keep your standards up against weaker opposition. That habit is what holds under pressure.
Find the point in a match where your level dips. Knowing it is most of fixing it.
One focus area at a time, but pick the one that breaks first when you are tired.

descriptions: Strong club-level control across the whole court, with clear tactical intent and few loose balls. Holding that level under sustained pressure is the remaining gap.
Control across the court and a clear plan behind the shots. Sustained pressure is what still moves your level.
Few loose balls, deliberate targeting, and a game that holds together against most club opposition.
You play with intent everywhere on the court. Prolonged pressure is the one thing that still finds a gap.
A complete club game, tactically aware. Maintaining it through a long match is the remaining work.
Strong control and clear intent. The gap now is durability rather than capability.
You rarely give anything away. What remains is holding that standard when the match goes long.
Whole-court control with real tactical shape. Pressure is the last variable.
This is a strong club standard. The remaining ground is measured in composure, not in shots.
Very few loose balls, and a plan behind most of them. Sustaining that is the final step.
summary: You set problems for most club opposition rather than solving theirs.
At this level the margins are small, and they sit mostly in the head rather than the hands.
Your game holds up against nearly everyone you will meet on a club night.
What separates you from the band above is what happens in the eleventh and twelfth points.
You have a complete club game. The work now is protecting it.
Opponents have to play well to beat you, which is not true of most players.
The remaining gains are narrow and specific, and worth chasing precisely.
Tactical clarity is already a weapon in your game.
You are past the stage where new shots help. Refinement is the route.
At this level, the player who holds their standard longest usually wins.
closing: This rating reflects where your game is today, not where it can go. Bring it back in a few months and expect the picture to have moved.
One focus area at a time is plenty. Come back for a reassessment once it starts to feel automatic.
Keep playing to your strengths while you work on the focus area — the fastest progress usually comes from doing both at once.
Play up whenever you can. Opposition is your best training tool now.
The remaining gains are small and specific. Pick one and be patient with it.
Come back for a reassessment after a run of competitive matches rather than social ones.
Protect what is already strong. At this level, losing a strength costs more than gaining one gives.
Train tired. That is where your remaining gap actually shows up.
Record a match if you can. At this level you will spot things nobody thought to tell you.
Progress slows here, and that is not a sign that anything is wrong.

descriptions: High club-level play: dependable execution, deliberate targeting and composure when exchanges speed up. Sets the terms of most rallies against club opposition.
Dependable under pressure, deliberate in targeting, and composed when the pace lifts. You dictate most club rallies.
A high club standard across the board, with the composure to hold it when exchanges get fast.
Execution, targeting and temperament all hold up. You set the terms rather than respond to them.
You control the shape of most rallies against club opposition, and the speed of them too.
Dependable everywhere, with the composure that separates the top of the club from the rest.
There is no obvious way through your game at club level. Rallies happen on your terms.
Strong across every phase, and steady when the exchanges speed up.
A high club standard: few weaknesses, clear intent, and composure under pace.
You are at the top of the club range, where the remaining gains are specialist rather than general.
summary: Very little at club level will trouble you, which makes finding a challenge the harder problem.
You dictate rallies rather than negotiate them.
At this level improvement comes from opposition more than from drills.
Your profile offers no easy way in for an opponent, which is rare.
The remaining gains are specialist and narrow, and they need deliberately seeking out.
You set the terms of most rallies you play in this club.
Composure under pace is already one of your strengths, and it is the rarest one.
Progress at this level is slow and precise, and worth the patience.
Most of your development now comes from who you choose to play, not what you practise.
You are at the point where partnering well matters as much as playing well.
closing: This rating reflects where your game is today, not where it can go. Bring it back in a few months and expect the picture to have moved.
One focus area at a time is plenty. Come back for a reassessment once it starts to feel automatic.
Keep playing to your strengths while you work on the focus area — the fastest progress usually comes from doing both at once.

Consider tournament play if you have not. Match pressure teaches what club nights cannot.
Your biggest gains may now come from your partner and your communication rather than your shots.
